September 28th, 1952
Flying Air France,
Paris to
Frankfort
Cher Jeunes Filles, Famille et mes Amis:
We are embarked on an expedition which confidentially
is definitely and positively against my better judgment. That is to say,
we are flying in Air France from Paris to Frankfort because we couldn't get
on a train and we have to be in Frankfort Monday morning. So far so good;
Our DC-4 is full of passengers, mostly Americans, many of whom are connected with
the Government of Harry Trumen, or his Armed Forces. They like to go do Paris
for the weekend and get back on the job Monday. No one can blame them for that,
but the one train and the one plane leaving Paris Sunday night are always packed.
PAA has influence with the airline (we do not operate Paris-Frankfort) but darn
little with the Wagon-Lits. We have just had a very gooå dinner with wine and
brandy. (The crew got the same rations! I hope the radio operator, flight
engineer, and co-pilot all like brandy and therefore don't pass their small
bottles along to the Captain who will make the landing - if any).
We've had a lot of fun in Paris, which is probably as
news-worthy a statement as to say that a 10 year old had fun at the Circus!
Last night we went up to Montmartre with the Wallace Whittakers where we looked
over some French watercolors and paintings, some modern and some good, and then
went to a nearby night club called Momseigneur where strolling minstrels play
with 14 violins all going at once and hard in a tiny room. Never have you
heard such music or seen so much excitement.
Later - October 2nd, flying via Sabena to Hamburg-
Dusseldorf, Brussels, London. Obviously we arrived
safely at Frankfort.
The following morning, Monday, September 29th, we flew to
Dusseldorf on P.A.A. 's local German Line and then cirove to Cologne where
Mr. Whittaker and I had some business. Our better halves did some shopping,

mostly of the window gazing variety. We had dinner and stayed the night at
the Hotel Excelsior and the next morning started out bright and early to motor
down the Rhine Valley to Bonn, Coblenz across the Rhine at Kolb (below the
Lorelei) and on to Wiesbaden. There we had late lunch at the Nassauer Hof, made
a few unsuccessful bets at the beautiful Casino and drove on to Frankfort. It
is a lovely drive all the way through little German towns many of which were
gaily decorated for the wine festival. Coblenz wes really smeared by Allied
bombers. The Cathedral was intect but the rest of the City is still pretty flat.
A few new buildings, but very few in contrast to Frankfort and other Cities which
are rapidly reconstructing those central areas such as around the bridges,
railroad station, and power plants which were, of course, the main targets of
air attack. Our P.A.A. driver was not only very good as a chauffeur but also
interesting. He is a Latvian, who escaped from the fussians, enlisted in the
French underground and has just recently returned from service in Indo-China where
he was with the Airborne Commandos. His job was to parachute down behind the
Red lines, blow up ammunition dumps, military stores and other such objectives
and then get back to his own lines by foot. He was badly wounded several times
and finally invalided home. He speaks English, Russian, French and German.
Arriving back at Frankfort we stayed overnight and the next
day, Wednesdey, October Ist, we put the show on the road again. This time we
left Frankfort at 3:30 PM on Scandanavian Airways and flew to Hamburg, spent the
night at the Atlantic Hotel - probably the finest in Europe. We had a marvelous
dinner wiih the Manager and his wife. They had many interesting stories to tell
about the War and how he had twice saved the hotel at the risk of his life by
putting out fires under a rain of bombs. The Whittakers had the "Hitler Suite"
(whenever he stayed there, Storm Troopers were assigned rooms all around him as
well as on the floors above and below). Debby and I had the suite occupies by
the Emperor of Japan, the Kaiser and other such. The following day, Thursday,

October 2nd, we made a short tour of Hamburg in the P.A.A. "Volkswagen" and
took a Sabena (Belgian Airline) to Dusseldorf, Brussels and London. We stayed
at Claridges in London Thursday and Friday nights and Saturday morning took
Air Chance to Paris. There I left the Madam safely ensconced in the Roblin
and caught a P.A.A. scheduled 8 P.M. departure for New York.
Later - enroute Gander-Boston. I have had an uneventful
crossing. Paris to Shannon, then Gander, Newfoundland and now we're over
Nova Scotia sparkling in brillant sunshine 10,000 feet below. On board is a
very interesting man who represents the wool growers of 13 Western States. The
U. S. Wool industry has been on the decline because of the scarcity of sheep
herders. It seems that our boys would rather take their girls to the movies
or hang around the corner drug store than wander off alone in the mountsins for
months at a time doing a pied piper routine with a lot of sheep. As a result
the wool growers association got some legislation through Congress to permit
the immigration of Basque sheep herders. Some 3000 will be flown all the way
from the Pyrenees to the Rockies. 500 will be flown this year starting tomorrow
and 2500 next year. All of them will fly with P.A.A. to New York and I.W.A.
across the U.S.A. Many of these boys have never ridden in an automobile. Most
of them speak only Bascue. We pin a big badge on each one which he is told is
his ticket. It tells where he is going and how. Also if he strays from the fold
the finder is asked in French and English to lead him Jo a P.A.A. office. In the
Test they receive $200. per month plus their board, lodgings, if any, tobacco and
a California wine, equivalent of Spanish wine. One Ranch owner told my friend
that these herders let their salaries accumulate for so many years that the
Rancher finally settles the account by taking them into partnership rather than
deplete his working capital by paying their back wages. He said that something
like 80% of our Western sheep herders are Basques. Its a nice piece of business
for P.A.A. because most of them will be carried when westbound loads are light
and the gross will be net.

Hope to be in New York for two or three days, then to
St. Louis for a couple of days, back to New York for a couple and then back to
Paris and on to Bangkok, Hongkong and Tokyo.
All the best to all of you.
H.M.B.

Bixby to his family, dated September 28 to October 6, 1952, en route from Paris to Frankfurt, Dusseldorf, Brussels, and London; includes description of trip on Air France Douglas DC-4, touring in Germany, return to Boston via Paris, Shannon, and Gander; mentions Wallace Whittaker.
